name: How Learning Works
author: Recurse
subject: humanities
description: The science behind spaced repetition, retrieval practice and other study methods that make memories last.

lesson.intro: Most people study in ways that feel productive but fade fast. Cognitive science has found methods that work much better, and they explain why Recurse asks before it shows and spaces your reviews over days and weeks. This pack covers how memories fade, what makes them last, and which popular study habits do not hold up.

sections.title: Forgetting, consolidation and sleep
sections.body:
In the 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables such as DAX and BOK, then measured how long it took to relearn them after delays from 20 minutes to a month. Nonsense syllables meant he could not lean on anything he already knew.

His results, published in 1885 and replicated many times since, form the forgetting curve: most forgetting happens within the first hours and days, and then the rate of loss slows down. Meaningful material fades more slowly than nonsense, but the shape is the same.

Two more findings matter for studying:

- Relearning is faster than first learning. Even when you cannot recall something, a trace remains, so a review restores it quickly.
- Each well-timed review makes the curve flatter, so the next drop takes longer.

Memories also keep changing after you study. Consolidation is the process that stabilizes a new memory over the following hours and days, and much of it happens during sleep. In deep sleep the brain replays recent experiences, which is thought to help move them into long-term storage. Losing sleep weakens consolidation, and a night without sleep also makes it harder to form new memories the next day.
sections.tip: Studying in the evening and then sleeping well is a good combination; an all-nighter before an exam is not.

check.question: Ebbinghaus found that relearning a list he could no longer recall took less time than learning it the first time. What does this show?
choices: He had simply become a faster reader of nonsense syllables
Short nonsense syllables are always easier the second time
A trace of the list remained even though he could not recall it
Forgetting had not yet started when he relearned the list
check.explanation: Ebbinghaus called this 'savings'. A memory you cannot retrieve can still leave a trace, which is why reviewing forgotten material is faster than learning it from scratch.

sections.title: Spacing and retrieval practice
sections.body:
Spaced repetition puts the forgetting curve to work. Instead of studying something many times in one sitting (massed practice, or cramming), you review it several times with gaps in between. For the same total study time, spaced practice gives much better long-term retention. Cramming can get you through tomorrow's test, but the material fades quickly afterwards.

The best gap grows with how long you need to remember. Reviewing a day later suits a test next week; knowledge you want a year from now needs gaps of weeks or months.

Retrieval practice means pulling information out of memory: answering questions, using flashcards, or writing what you remember on a blank page. The act of recall strengthens a memory more than looking at the answer again. This is the testing effect. In a well-known 2006 study by Roediger and Karpicke, students who reread a passage did slightly better on a test five minutes later, but students who practised recalling it remembered much more a week later. Retrieval also shows you honestly what you do and do not know.

Recurse combines both. It asks before it shows the answer, and a scheduler called FSRS estimates how likely you are to recall each card, bringing it back when that chance falls to your target, 90% by default. Each successful recall makes the memory more durable, so the gaps grow from days to weeks to months.

check.question: Which of these is a form of retrieval practice?
choices: Reading through your notes again slowly and carefully
Covering your notes and writing down what you remember
Highlighting the most important sentences in a chapter
Listening to a recording of the lecture a second time
check.explanation: Retrieval practice means producing information from memory. Writing what you remember from a blank page counts; rereading, highlighting and relistening only expose you to the material again.

sections.title: Desirable difficulties: interleaving and elaboration
sections.body:
The psychologist Robert Bjork coined the term desirable difficulties for conditions that make learning feel slower and harder in the moment but improve long-term retention. Spacing and retrieval are two of them. The key idea is that performance during practice is not the same as learning: smooth, easy practice can feel like progress while building little that lasts.

Interleaving means mixing different kinds of problems in one session (A, C, B, A, B, C) instead of blocking them (A, A, A, B, B, B). Blocked practice feels easier because you know which method to use before you read each problem. Interleaving forces you to decide which method fits, which is exactly what a real test demands. In one maths study, students who interleaved problem types scored about three times higher on a test a week later (63% versus 20%), even though they did worse during practice. Interleaving helps most when the categories are similar and easy to confuse.

Elaboration means connecting new material to what you already know: asking how and why, comparing ideas, and making up your own examples. The Feynman technique, named after the physicist Richard Feynman, is a popular way to do it:

- Explain the idea in plain words, as if to a beginner.
- Notice where your explanation gets vague or stalls.
- Go back to the source to fill that gap, then explain it again more simply.

A difficulty is desirable only if you can overcome it with effort. Problems far beyond your current knowledge just cause frustration; step back to simpler material first.

check.question: Which study habit is an example of elaboration?
choices: Copying each definition out word for word into a notebook
Reading the whole chapter a second time before the test
Highlighting every key sentence in the chapter in yellow
Asking why a fact is true and linking it to something you know
check.explanation: Elaboration connects new material to existing knowledge by asking how and why and by generating examples. Copying, rereading and highlighting keep you on the surface of the text.

sections.title: Working memory and cognitive load
sections.body:
Working memory is the mental workspace that holds what you are thinking about right now, such as a phone number you are about to dial. It is small and brief: adults can hold only about four chunks of new information at once (an older estimate was seven, plus or minus two), and without rehearsal the contents fade within seconds. Long-term memory, by contrast, has no practical limit.

A chunk is a meaningful unit. The digits 1, 9, 8, 9 are four items to a young child but one chunk, a year, to someone who knows history. Experts are not better at everything; they have built large, organized chunks in long-term memory that let them handle more at once in their field.

Cognitive load theory, developed by John Sweller, describes the demands placed on working memory:

- Intrinsic load comes from the material itself: how many elements must be held together. It depends on what you already know.
- Extraneous load comes from how material is presented: cluttered slides, text split from the diagram it explains, notifications pulling your attention away.
- Germane load is the effort spent actually building understanding.

Good learning design cuts extraneous load and breaks complex topics into smaller steps. Worked examples help beginners because they show each step without forcing a search for a method; as skill grows, solving problems yourself becomes more useful.

check.question: Who tends to benefit most from studying worked examples?
choices: Beginners, because examples cut the load of searching for a method
Experts, because they can skim the examples quickly and move on
Everyone equally, whatever their level of skill or experience
No one, because examples replace the real thinking learners need
check.explanation: For novices, a worked example shows each step without the heavy load of searching for a method. As skill grows the benefit shrinks, and solving problems yourself becomes more useful.

sections.title: Myths: learning styles, rereading and highlighting
sections.body:
Some of the most popular beliefs about studying do not hold up.

Learning styles. Many people believe they are visual, auditory or kinesthetic learners and should be taught that way. People do have preferences, but a 2008 review by Pashler and colleagues found almost no well-designed evidence that matching teaching to a preferred style improves learning. A better rule is to match the format to the content (a map for geography, audio for pronunciation) and to combine words with pictures for everyone.

Rereading. Reading notes again makes the text feel familiar and easy to process. That fluency is easily mistaken for knowing the material, an illusion of competence: recognizing a page is far easier than recalling it. A large 2013 review by Dunlosky and colleagues rated rereading as a low-utility technique.

Highlighting. Highlighting is quick and feels productive, but the same review rated it low utility too. It is passive and can draw attention to isolated phrases instead of how ideas connect.

The review rated practice testing and distributed (spaced) practice as the two most useful techniques, with interleaving, elaborative interrogation (asking why) and self-explanation in the middle. A quick test for any study method: does it make you produce answers from memory, spread out over time? If not, it is probably weaker than it feels.

check.question: A large 2013 review of study techniques rated which of these as highly useful?
choices: Highlighting text
Practice testing
Rereading notes
Summarizing text
check.explanation: Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing and distributed practice as high utility. Highlighting, rereading and summarizing were all rated low utility.

keyTerms.definition: The pattern in which memory drops quickly soon after learning and then more slowly, unless it is reviewed.
The process, much of it during sleep, that stabilizes a new memory and integrates it into long-term storage.
Reviewing material several times with growing gaps between reviews instead of all at once.
The finding that retrieving information from memory strengthens it more than restudying it.
Mixing different types of problems or topics within one practice session.
A challenge during learning, such as spacing or testing, that slows practice but improves long-term retention.
The small, short-lived mental workspace that holds what you are thinking about right now.
The demand a task places on working memory.

summary: Forgetting is fastest right after learning; each well-timed review flattens the curve.
Spacing reviews over time and recalling answers from memory beat cramming and rereading.
Interleaving and elaboration feel harder but build learning that lasts and transfers.
Working memory holds only a few chunks, so cut clutter and build knowledge step by step.
Sleep consolidates memories; learning styles, rereading and highlighting are weaker than they feel.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why answering a flashcard from memory a few days from now will help them more than rereading their notes three times tonight.

questions.question: What did Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve show?
choices: Memories fade at a steady rate, losing the same amount each day
Forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows down
Forgetting begins only about a week after learning
Material learned once is kept for life if it was understood
questions.explanation: Ebbinghaus lost much of each list within the first day, after which the rate of loss slowed. A steady rate is the common misreading. Meaningful material fades more slowly than nonsense syllables, but it still fades without review.

questions.question: Which German psychologist first measured the forgetting curve, publishing his results in 1885?
questions.explanation: Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and measured how much faster he could relearn them after different delays. His curve has been replicated many times since.

questions.question: A student plans to stay up all night reviewing before an exam. Based on sleep research, what is the main problem with this plan?
choices: Sleep plays no part in memory, so the only cost is feeling tired
Memories are stored only while awake, so extra hours awake help
Skipping sleep weakens consolidation and hurts next-day memory and focus
All-night study works as long as the student rereads everything twice
questions.explanation: During sleep, especially deep sleep, the brain stabilizes recently learned material. A night without sleep also leaves attention and the ability to form new memories impaired the next day, so the extra hours are bought at a high price.

questions.question: Two students each spend three hours on a topic. One studies in a single evening; the other does three one-hour sessions spread over a week. Who is likely to remember more a month later?
choices: The single-evening student, because the material was learned in one go
Both about the same, because their total study time was equal
The single-evening student, as long as the session ended with a review
The student who spread the sessions over a week
questions.explanation: This is the spacing effect: with equal total time, spreading study out produces far more durable memory than massing it. Cramming can work for a test the next morning, but the material fades quickly afterwards.

questions.question: What is the name for the finding that recalling information from memory strengthens it more than restudying it?
questions.explanation: The testing effect, also called the retrieval practice effect, shows that recall is itself a learning event, not just a check of what you know.

questions.question: In a 2006 study, students either reread a passage or practised recalling it. Rereading gave slightly better scores on a test five minutes later. What happened on a test one week later?
choices: Both groups scored about the same
The rereading group kept its lead
The recall group remembered substantially more
Both groups had forgotten nearly everything
questions.explanation: After a week, the students who had practised recall remembered far more, about 56% of the ideas against 42%. Rereading gives a short-term boost and a feeling of fluency, but retrieval builds memory that lasts.

questions.question: Why does a spaced repetition system like Recurse wait longer before showing a card again each time you recall it correctly?
choices: Each correct recall makes the memory more durable, so it fades more slowly
Cards you already know are treated as less important to the course
Longer gaps exist mainly so the app can fit more new cards into each day
A memory stops fading for good once you have recalled it correctly twice
questions.explanation: Each successful retrieval makes a memory more stable, so it takes longer to fall to the point where review is needed. Reviewing near that point gives the most benefit for the least time. Memories never stop fading entirely, which is why reviews continue at longer intervals.

questions.question: Explain why Recurse asks you to answer before it shows the answer, instead of simply showing you the facts to reread.
questions.answer: Pulling an answer out of memory is itself a learning event: effortful retrieval strengthens the memory and makes it easier to retrieve next time. Rereading only feels productive because the material looks familiar, and it gives no honest signal of what you could recall on your own.
questions.explanation: This is the testing effect. Answering first also tells the scheduler how well you know each card, so it can space the next review appropriately.

questions.question: A student preparing for a geometry test can do 10 area problems, then 10 volume problems, then 10 angle problems, or shuffle all 30 together. Which approach does research favour, and why?
choices: Shuffling, because choosing the method for each problem is part of the skill
Blocks, because repeating one method many times builds fluency fastest
Blocks, because mixing several topics at once overloads working memory
Either way, because only the total amount of practice time matters
questions.explanation: Interleaving forces you to decide which method fits each problem, which is what a test demands. In one study it roughly tripled scores a week later, even though practice felt harder and went worse. Blocked practice feels fluent only because you know the method before reading each problem.

questions.question: What term did psychologist Robert Bjork coin for conditions that make learning feel harder but improve long-term retention?
questions.explanation: Desirable difficulties include spacing, retrieval practice and interleaving. They slow apparent progress during practice but produce learning that lasts. A difficulty is desirable only if the learner can overcome it with effort.

questions.question: Which step is at the heart of the Feynman technique?
choices: Copying the textbook's explanation word for word until it sticks
Reading an expert's summary several times before a test
Memorizing key terms with a mnemonic before learning their meaning
Explaining the idea simply, then fixing the parts where it breaks down
questions.explanation: The method is to explain the concept in plain words as if to a beginner, notice where you get vague or stuck, go back to the source and try again. It combines retrieval with elaboration and exposes gaps that rereading hides.

questions.question: Explain the difference between performance during practice and learning, and why it matters when choosing study methods.
questions.answer: Performance is how well you do while practising; learning is the lasting change that shows up later. Cramming, blocked practice and rereading boost performance in the moment but fade, while spacing, retrieval and interleaving feel slower yet give better long-term results, so how practice feels is a poor guide to what works.
questions.explanation: Bjork's distinction explains why learners often prefer weaker methods: they judge by how fluent practice feels. The real test is what you can do days or weeks later.

questions.question: Why is a long list of unfamiliar terms hard to learn in a single pass?
choices: Long-term memory has limited room and fills up quickly with new words
New words can only be stored during sleep, not while you are reading
Working memory holds only a few new chunks, so new items push out old ones
The brain automatically filters out information it has never seen before
questions.explanation: Working memory can hold only about four chunks of new information at a time. Long-term memory has no practical limit, so the bottleneck is getting items through working memory, which is why small sets and repeated review work better.

questions.question: A diagram is on one slide and its explanation is on the next, so learners must flip back and forth to connect them. What kind of load does this add?
choices: Intrinsic load, because the topic itself is complex and difficult
Extraneous load, because the layout rather than the content creates it
Germane load, because the extra effort deepens your understanding
No extra load at all, because each slide is simple on its own
questions.explanation: Extraneous load comes from how material is presented, not from the material itself. Holding the diagram in mind while reading separate text wastes working memory; putting the explanation on the diagram removes that load.

questions.question: What is the name for grouping separate items into a larger meaningful unit, such as remembering the digits 1, 9, 8, 9 as the year 1989?
questions.explanation: Chunking lets working memory hold more by treating several items as one. Experts handle complex material easily because long-term memory supplies them with large, well-organized chunks.

questions.question: What does research show about teaching people in their preferred 'learning style', such as visual, auditory or kinesthetic?
choices: Well-controlled studies find little or no benefit from matching
Matching teaching to a learner's style reliably doubles retention
Only visual learners benefit, because most people think in images
Styles matter a great deal for children but not for adults
questions.explanation: People do have preferences, but a 2008 review by Pashler and colleagues found almost no well-designed evidence that matching instruction to a preferred style improves learning. Matching the format to the content, and combining words with pictures for everyone, works better.

questions.question: Why do rereading and highlighting feel effective even though they produce little lasting learning?
choices: They do strengthen recall, but only when done right before a test
They work well, but only for people who are mainly visual learners
They take so long that students assume they must be learning something
Familiar text feels easy to process, and the ease is mistaken for mastery
questions.explanation: Seeing material again makes it feel fluent and familiar, an illusion of competence, but recognizing text is much easier than recalling it. A large 2013 review rated both rereading and highlighting as low-utility techniques.
